questions.q: What is the actual mechanism behind parameter sniffing?
options: SQL Server compiles a plan optimized for the first parameter value it sees, caches that plan, and reuses it for subsequent calls even when a very different value is supplied
SQL Server recompiles a fresh plan for every single execution automatically
It only happens when statistics have never been updated
It is caused exclusively by using table variables instead of temp tables
questions.explain: The plan is built and cached around whichever value triggered the first compile; a skewed data distribution then makes that cached plan a poor fit for other values.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the decisive test to confirm parameter sniffing rather than stale statistics?
options: Run the query with OPTION (RECOMPILE) to force a fresh compile using the current call's actual value; if it's dramatically better with statistics already confirmed current, it's sniffing
Restart the SQL Server service and see if performance changes
Check whether the query uses a JOIN or a subquery
Rebuild every index on the database and measure again
questions.explain: OPTION (RECOMPILE) bypasses the cached plan and compiles fresh for that specific value; a dramatic improvement with current stats isolates the cause to the cached plan itself, not the statistics.

options: Forces the optimizer to always compile as if that specific value were supplied, regardless of the actual parameter value passed at runtime
Deletes the cached plan permanently from the plan cache
Updates statistics only for rows matching that value
Forces a table scan instead of an index seek for that value
questions.explain: OPTIMIZE FOR pins compilation to a chosen representative value (or UNKNOWN for average density), stabilizing the plan regardless of what value is actually passed.

questions.q: What does Parameter Sensitive Plan (PSP) optimization, introduced in SQL Server 2022, do differently?
options: It allows the optimizer to automatically cache multiple plan variants for the same query based on parameter value ranges, instead of forcing one plan to serve every case
It disables parameter sniffing entirely across all SQL Server versions back to 2008
It removes the need for indexes on parameterized queries
It only works for queries that use OPTION (RECOMPILE) explicitly
questions.explain: PSP directly targets the classic skewed-distribution sniffing problem by letting SQL Server keep several plan shapes cached, chosen based on the incoming parameter value's range.

questions.q: What is the tradeoff of using OPTION (RECOMPILE) as a fix for parameter sniffing?
options: It guarantees the best plan for every call, but pays compilation overhead on every single execution, making it best for infrequently run queries
It permanently disables statistics updates for that table
It can only be applied at the database level, never per query
It has no downside and should always be the first fix attempted for every query
questions.explain: Recompiling on every call avoids a mismatched cached plan entirely, but the constant compilation cost makes it best suited to queries where that overhead is trivial compared to execution cost.
